title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline, Revision 2026
journal: Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy 2026;56(4)
breakthrough: APTA Orthopedics and the APTA Hand and Upper Extremity Academy jointly revised the carpal tunnel syndrome guideline, linked to the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health. Clinicians should use the CTS-6 to help diagnose suspected carpal tunnel syndrome; the Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire Symptom Severity Scale at baseline and at least one further point including discharge to track symptom change; and either the DASH or QuickDASH to track function, in both surgically and non-surgically managed patients.
impact: Separates the three jobs that get conflated in practice — diagnosing, tracking symptoms and tracking function — and assigns a specific instrument to each. The ICF linkage means outcomes are expressed as function rather than as nerve conduction velocity.
practical: Adopt the measurement set: CTS-6 to diagnose, BCTQ symptom severity at baseline and follow-up, DASH or QuickDASH for function. The DASH requirement is the one most often missed — symptom scores alone will not show whether a hand is working better. Diagnostic accuracy for the CTS-6 rests on limited evidence, alongside the Kamath and Stothard questionnaire and the Katz and Stirrat hand diagram, so it supports rather than replaces clinical reasoning.
link: JOSPT — Hand Pain and Sensory Deficits: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome, Revision 2026

verify.status: matched with corrections — real, one instrument missing and 'mandates' softened
verify.note: Verified: JOSPT 2026;56(4), doi 10.2519/jospt.2026.0301, published April 2026, jointly revised by APTA Orthopedics and the APTA Hand and Upper Extremity Academies, ICF-linked, with the CTS-6 recommended for diagnosis and the BCTQ Symptom Severity Scale at baseline plus at least one follow-up. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) The DASH or QuickDASH recommendation for assessing FUNCTION was missing from the submission, which lists only CTS-6 and BCTQ — an incomplete measurement set is the most likely way this guideline gets implemented wrongly. (2) The submission says the guideline 'Mandates standardized baseline and outcome evaluation... prior to electrodiagnostic testing or surgical referral'. These are recommendations linked to instruments, and the sequencing relative to electrodiagnostic testing as stated could not be confirmed; reworded to what the guideline recommends. Added that CTS-6 diagnostic accuracy rests on limited evidence, which the guideline itself notes. YEAR: correctly assigned to 2026 — the guideline is titled Revision 2026 and published April 2026.

title: First Breakthrough Device Designation for a Brain-Computer Interface in Stroke Motor Rehabilitation
breakthrough: The FDA granted Breakthrough Device Designation to CorTec's Brain Interchange system for direct cortical electrical stimulation to support motor recovery in chronic stroke-related impairment — the first brain-computer interface worldwide to receive the designation for stroke motor rehabilitation. The system is fully implantable and wireless, designed for long-term neural recording with adaptive closed-loop stimulation. It is being evaluated in an FDA-approved IDE study at the University of Washington, the first clinical investigation of a fully implantable wireless BCI for stroke rehabilitation in humans, following 510(k) clearance of the company's cortical mapping electrodes in 2019 and a 2023 feasibility demonstration of beta-phase-locked closed-loop stimulation.
impact: Signals that regulators regard closed-loop cortical stimulation as a plausible route to recovery in patients whose motor function has plateaued — a group conventional rehabilitation currently discharges.
practical: Nothing changes in clinic yet, and it is important to say why. Breakthrough Device Designation expedites FDA interaction and review; it does not alter the requirements for marketing authorisation and does not guarantee approval, and this device remains investigational under an IDE. The realistic near-term role for a physiatrist is identifying and referring candidates to the trial, not prescribing the therapy.
link: CorTec receives FDA Breakthrough Device Designation for its Brain Interchange system in stroke rehabilitation

verify.status: corrected — a designation was described as a change in clinical guidelines
verify.note: Verified: FDA Breakthrough Device Designation announced April 2026 for CorTec's Brain Interchange system, the first BCI worldwide designated for stroke motor rehabilitation, fully implantable and wireless, under FDA-approved IDE study at the University of Washington, with 2019 510(k) clearance of cortical mapping electrodes and a 2023 beta-phase-locked closed-loop feasibility study. CORRECTION: both submitted lists say the designation 'Re-defines neuro-rehabilitation frameworks by integrating implantable bidirectional neural recording and adaptive stimulation into clinical stroke recovery guidelines' and 'Provides physiatrists with a bioelectronic tool'. Neither is true yet — this is an investigational device with an expedited-review designation, no guideline includes it, and the announcement itself states that the designation does not change the requirements for marketing authorisation and does not guarantee approval. Rewritten so the regulatory status is unambiguous, since 'provides physiatrists with a tool' would have a clinician looking for something they cannot obtain. YEAR: correctly assigned to 2026 — the designation is April 2026.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Needle EMG for Nerve Transfer Candidacy in Cervical Spinal Cord Injury
breakthrough: Combining neuromuscular ultrasound with needle electromyography improves muscle localisation and patient safety when mapping donor and recipient muscles in complex nerve injury, including the upper limb in cervical spinal cord injury. The muscles examined for donor and recipient nerve-muscle combinations include teres minor, serratus anterior, brachialis, supinator, extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, flexor pollicis longus and extensor indicis. The supinator is a particularly valuable donor — its radial nerve branch transferred to the posterior interosseous nerve restores thumb and finger extension in patients with C5 to C7 level injuries. Normal preoperative manual muscle testing of a donor corresponded with intraoperative nerve stimulation and normal nerve architecture on postoperative histopathology.
impact: Makes the preoperative electrodiagnostic assessment reliable enough to trust for donor selection. A subclinically denervated donor looks adequate on examination and fails after transfer, and the operation is not repeatable.
practical: Know which operation is being planned, because the assessment differs: this work concerns NERVE transfer, where a donor nerve is rerouted to reinnervate a paralysed muscle, not tendon transfer, where an intact muscle-tendon unit is moved. The supinator-to-PIN transfer for thumb and finger extension in C5 to C7 injury is the concrete example to know. Ultrasound guidance is described as a valuable adjunct to needle localisation rather than a mandated standard.
link: Muscle & Nerve — ultrasound guidance to augment needle electromyography precision in the complex nerve injury setting

verify.status: corrected — wrong operation named, and 'mandatory standard' is not supported
verify.note: The work is real: Mayo Clinic uses preoperative ultrasound-guided needle EMG for upper-limb reconstruction planning in cervical spinal cord injury, and the technique paper is in Muscle & Nerve 2026 (Saddler et al., doi 10.1002/mus.70100). TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) WRONG OPERATION. Both submitted lists describe this as assessing candidacy for TENDON TRANSFER. The Mayo material and the muscle list concern NERVE transfer — the supinator branch of the radial nerve to the posterior interosseous nerve for thumb and finger extension in C5-7 injury is the worked example. Tendon transfer moves an intact muscle-tendon unit; nerve transfer reinnervates a paralysed muscle. They have different candidacy criteria, so this is a substantive error rather than a wording slip. (2) 'Establishing ultrasound-guided EMG as a mandatory preoperative diagnostic standard' overstates it; the publication describes ultrasound as a valuable tool to augment muscle localisation and enhance safety. Also corrected 'clinical trial data' — this is a technique and practice report, not a trial. YEAR: correctly assigned to 2026.
